description: Hi, I am a video game enthusiast who enjoys simulating real world interactions through a variety of platforms.
summary: Red Base: Jezero is a 3D browser game where kids aged 7–12 run a Mars outpost at Jezero Crater for five days. Mars gets only 43% of the sunlight Earth does, so the base never has enough power. Each morning the player gets a few power cells and decides where they go: life support, the digger that builds radiation shielding, or the science lab. Those decisions decide what happens next. If the shelter isn’t shielded when a solar storm arrives, the crew takes radiation damage. The storms are based on real solar flares from NASA’s DONKI space-weather database. If life support goes without power, air and food start running out. Dust storms cut solar power, and the batteries have to last through cold nights. At the end of the mission, players see how their choices played out and can try again with a different plan.
details:
Playspace’s Project Solution
Red Base: Jezero is a free 3D game that runs in a web browser. It uses NASA and Canadian Space Agency data to put kids in charge of a Mars outpost, where they have to balance life support, radiation shielding, power and food.

How the game works:
The mission lasts five days on Mars. Every morning the Power Hub hands out a limited number of power cells, and the player carries each one to a system. Each day adds a new problem.

Power (Mars sunlight):
Mars is about 1.5 times farther from the Sun than Earth, so solar panels there collect about 43% as much energy. We worked this out from NASA’s Mars Fact Sheet. In the game, there are always more systems than cells, so the player has to pick.

Radiation storms (NASA DONKI):
A solar storm hits on Day 2. Each storm in the game is based on a real flare from NASA’s DONKI database, and the game also checks DONKI to see how active the Sun has been lately. If the player powered the Regolith Digger, Martian soil has been piled onto the shelter, which blocks radiation. If they called Earth on the radio, they got an early warning, delayed by the real Earth–Mars signal time. A player who did neither takes 50% more damage. On normal days, the crew still picks up about 0.64 millisieverts a day outside, the dose NASA’s Curiosity rover measured.

Life support and food (Canadian Space Agency):
With Life Support powered, the greenhouse grows red romaine lettuce, dwarf tomatoes and chile peppers, the same crops astronauts have grown on the International Space Station. Players harvest them, put them in the fridge and pick meals in the kitchen. The nutrition info comes from the Canadian Space Agency’s food-production toolkit. Fresh food is better for health and morale, but packaged pouches last longer.

Dust storms and cold nights:
On Days 3 and 4, a dust storm blocks the sun and solar power drops. This is based on the 2018 global dust storm that ended NASA’s Opportunity rover mission. Whatever the batteries stored during the day has to keep the heaters running overnight.

Science at Jezero:
Powering the Lab lets players scan and analyze rocks to reach the mission’s science goal. Jezero was a lake billions of years ago, and Perseverance is searching it for signs of past life.

Seeing the results:
Each night, a recap lists what the player chose and what happened because of it. At the end, they get a 1–3 star rating, a short story of their mission and a tip for a different strategy. There are four specialist roles, three difficulty levels and a Retry Day button, so players can try new approaches.

Real Mars events:
Players can also step into real moments: Opportunity’s 2018 dust storm, a 2017 solar storm, a dust devil filmed by the Spirit rover, Ingenuity’s first flight, and a blue sunset photographed by Curiosity. The game opens with a launch based on the Artemis I timeline. There is also an in-game tablet with quizzes and a mission journal.

Benefits

  • Kids practice making decisions with limited resources.
  • Real NASA data shows up as storms, sunlight and radiation they have to deal with, instead of charts.
  • It’s free and runs in a browser with no download or login, including on school Chromebooks.
  • With the fact that the game can run on the browser, it also includes detailed sound design for enhanced immersion as well as visually appealing graphics for visual stimulation.

Our goal
We wanted kids to get a feel for what running a Mars mission is like, using real data. To keep it understandable for ages 7–12, we simplified a few things: shorter days, simpler radiation math and a small crew. An in-game “What’s simplified” page explains each change. Later versions could add a Moon base, multiplayer crews and a teacher dashboard.

Tools and Technologies Used

Coding languages:

  • JavaScript, HTML and CSS

Graphics and sound:

  • three.js (WebGL) for the 3D graphics, lighting and effects
  • Web Audio API for sound effects made in code

Data sources:

  • NASA DONKI: real solar flares from 2017–2025 for the radiation storms, plus recent activity
  • NASA Mars Fact Sheet: sunlight strength and Earth–Mars distance
  • NASA Curiosity RAD: daily radiation dose on Mars
  • NASA/USGS Viking color map: the surface of Mars in the launch and landing scenes
  • Canadian Space Agency food-production toolkit: crops and nutrition
